1. Introduction

Background and Motivation

Energy efficiency in campus buildings is a critical concern, with HVAC and lighting systems accounting for a
significant portion of operational costs and carbon emissions. Traditional occupancy detection methods—such as
manual switches or basic motion sensors—often fail to accurately detect the number and presence of occupants,
especially in dynamic, multi-person environments. This leads to unnecessary energy consumption and reduced
occupant comfort 4 5 6.

Recent advances in sensor technology, particularly the emergence of low-cost Doppler radar (e.g., LD2450) and
thermal array sensors, offer new opportunities for precise, privacy-preserving, and real-time occupancy detection.

When integrated with automated power control systems, these sensors can enable intelligent, demand-driven
energy management at the room or zone level, maximizing savings while maintaining comfort 4 5 6.

2. Sensor Technologies for Multi-Person Occupancy Detection
LD2450 Radar Sensors: Principles and Performance

The LD2450 is a Doppler radar sensor capable of detecting fine-grained motion, including human breathing and
micro-movements, making it highly sensitive to occupancy—even when individuals are stationary 7 . Key
advancements include:

¢ High Sensitivity: Detects small motions, outperforming PIR in stationary scenarios.

¢ Coverage Pattern: Sensitivity varies with range and placement; careful calibration is required 7 .

¢ Occlusion Handling: Recent designs use MIMO radar and advanced signal processing (e.g., CFAR, matched

filtering) to improve multi-person detection and reduce false alarms in cluttered environments 8 9.
¢ Integration: Well-suited for privacy-critical spaces due to non-imaging nature.
Limitations: Sensitivity variation across range, potential for multipath artifacts, and higher cost compared to PIR
or low-res thermal sensors 7 .

Thermal array sensors detect infrared radiation, mapping temperature distributions to identify human presence.
Their performance is highly dependent on resolution:

¢ Low-Resolution (e.g., 8x8): Cost-effective, privacy-preserving, and sufficient for basic occupancy detection and
activity recognition. Achieves up to 99% accuracy with machine learning, but struggles with closely spaced

individuals and occlusion 1 10.

¢ High-Resolution (e.g., 24x32): Enables accurate multi-person detection, tracking, and occlusion handling. Deep

learning models (e.g., YOLOv5, DETR) achieve >97% accuracy for up to three people u .
¢ Privacy: No visual imagery, making them suitable for sensitive environments 10.
¢ Cost and Power: Higher resolutions increase cost and processing requirements.

Limitations: Performance degrades with thick clothing, occlusion, or more occupants than trained for; sensor
placement and frame rate are critical 1 .

Machine Learning for Multi-Person Detection
Advanced machine learning models have revolutionized occupancy detection:

¢ YOLOv5/DETR: Adapted for low-res thermal data, these models achieve >98% mean average precision (mAP)
for multi-person localization, with YOLOvSm offering real-time processing and small model size 122 13 .

¢ ViTPose++: Transformer-based models excel in pose estimation, outperforming YOLOv8 in complex scenarios
with occlusion and diverse postures 13 .

¢ Data Augmentation: Synthetic data generation and transfer learning enable generalization across room sizes

and sensor placements 122 14.

Challenges: Performance drops with occlusion, thick clothing, or more occupants than the model was trained on;
requires labeled data for training 2 15 .

Sensor Fusion Strategies
Combining LD2450 radar and thermal arrays leverages complementary strengths:

¢ Experimental Results: Sensor fusion achieves up to 99% accuracy in multi-person detection, outperforming

single-modality systems 2 16.

¢ Fusion Methods: Low-level fusion (occupancy grids), deep neural networks, and probabilistic filters (e.g.,

SMC-PHD) enhance robustness and reduce false positives 2 17.

¢ Mitigation of Limitations: Fusion compensates for occlusion, sensitivity variation, and stationary occupant

detection issues inherent in individual sensors 16 .

3. Multi-Person Detection Accuracy and Reliability

Comparative Accuracy of Sensor Technologies

¢ LD2450 Radar: High accuracy for motion and stationary detection (e.g., breathing), but sensitive to placement

and environmental factors 1s 19.

¢ Thermal Arrays: High accuracy (up to 99%) with ML, especially at higher resolutions; robust to lighting and

privacy concerns 20 21.

¢ PIR/RFID: Alone, PIR is limited (cannot detect stationary occupants); fusion with RFID or thermal arrays
boosts accuracy to ~94-99% 22 23.

¢ Environmental Sensors: CO2, VOCs, and temperature sensors combined with ML can estimate occupancy with

80-99% accuracy, but with latency and indirectness 24 25.
